content_html_sanitized:
Oh, surely my headline is hyperbole. Nope, it’s an understatement.

Today I found this headline on Bloomberg.com, Effort to Ease Cannabis Rules Faces New Opposition From Experts.

The Bloomberg report is based on an article in the Journal of the American Medical Association,the psychiatric division.

Rescheduling Cannabis—Medicine or Politics?

First, understanding that headlines are not always written by the author, but a claim of expertise should always raise questions. “Experts” at what? 

“An argument from authority is a form of argument in which the opinion of an authority figure (or figures) who lacks relevant expertise is used as evidence to support an argument.The argument from authority is an informal fallacy,and obtaining knowledge in this way is fallible.” 

So who are these “experts”? Bertha K. Madras, PhD, has a degree in psychobiology. That does not make her an expert on economics, or sociology, or policing, or history or even the medical use of cannabis. Nonetheless, it was published in the psychiatric part of JAMA.

From 2004, See California Addiction Specialist Lies to Justify Cannabis Prohibition and War on Sick and Dying. Misrepresents JAMA Articles.

That does not keep her from arguing against sick and dying Americans being being allowed the medical use of cannabis: “Finally, the US Food and Drug Administration has not approved cannabis as a medicine, as evidence is deficient in several key areas, including data from high-quality clinical trials, standardized cannabis formulations, established purity, defined routes of administration, dosing guidelines, and specific frequencies of use.”

After all, the FDA has only had almost three decades since Proposition 215 passed in 1996 to do the basic research that she expects. Did the marijuana reform movement delay this research? Or did NIDA and the DEA, and/or especially the Drug Czar’s office.

Certainly, we should not expect Cannabis to be taken out of Schedule 1 , along with  heroin, LSD, methamphetamine, methaqualone.without it being given the same scrutiny it was given in 1970, when Richard Nixon directed his Attorney General, John Mitchell, to put it in Schedule 1 without any scientific evidence. Mitchel later went to prison because of his involvement in the Watergate scandal.

Obviously, there was never any scientific basis for that action and it should not have been in Schedule 1 in the first place. 

In any case, there’s this from 1998:

DEA FINALLY CONFIRMS THE EXISTENCE OF SUFFICIENT GROUNDS TO REMOVE MARIJUANA FROM HARD DRUGS SCHEDULE OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES

At least, she is too modest to recommend what the punishments should be for AIDS or cancer patients for brazenly ignoring her opinions as an expert on psychobiology.

It is my opinion as a person with a degree in economics from Yale University that she suffers from delusions of grandeur and needs psychotherapy. 

Why not? I am as qualified to say that as she is to demand that patients should be subject to arrest until the DEA and NIDA agree to fact check a deceased Watergate conspirator. 

And then there is Paul J. Larkin, JD . https://www.heritage.org/staff/paul-j-larkin who is a lawyer who used to work for the Drug Czar’s office, and who now works for the Heritage Foundation. In short, he is a professional Prohibitionist, who has opposed even medical cannabis. Does that make him an expert? 

The Heritage Foundation  is a longtime supporter of cannabis prohibition, including opposition to medical cannabis and it really does blatantly lie about it, and me. See How The Heritage Foundation Used Newsweek to Recycle Lies About My “Medical Marijuana Scam”

In the meantime, countries that have legalized medical cannabis include Albania, Argentina, Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Ecuador, Finland, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Jamaica, Lebanon, Luxembourg, Malawi, Malta, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Panama, Peru, Poland, Portugal, Rwanda, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, San Marino, South Africa, Spain, Sri Lanka, Switzerland, Thailand, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Uruguay, Vanuatu, Zambia, and Zimbabwe…

In the United States, 39 states, 4 territories, and the District of Columbia have legalized the medical use of cannabis, but at the federal level its use remains prohibited, because it is still in Nixon’s Schedule One.  

Someone needs psychotherapy, and/or a new headline writer.
